rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative ending on al-malāʾika is a canonical variant of the preceding word and may reparse the clause structure.
rows.anchor: Same variant as word 5 — the nominative ending on malāʾika precedes the imperative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural We replaces singular I in a canonical reading, changing divine voice but not meaning and retaining Form IV causation.
rows.anchor: Shifts from singular ""I"" to plural ""We"" (royal plural) — changes divine voice but not meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second-person singular reading addresses Muhammad, shifting from divine self-declaration to prophetic characterization.
rows.anchor: Second person singular ""you were not"" — shifts speaker from God to addressing Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person plural reading makes God speak directly, replacing third-person narrative report with divine announcement.
rows.anchor: First person plural ""We say"" — shifts speaker from third-person God to direct divine voice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza's canonical reading simplifies the hamza in qurʾān, reflecting dialectal pronunciation without a stated semantic difference.
rows.anchor: Hamza simplification: dropping hamza from qurʾān to qurān; attested canonical variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the seven canonical readings, qibalan means facing them from the front, stressing directional confrontation rather than manner.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant (seven readings): qibalan means ""from the front, facing them"" — spatial emphasis

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Hamza reading explicitly realizes hamza instead of wāw, sharply marking the glottal stop without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Hamza variant: explicit hamza instead of waw — emphasizes the glottal stop

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternative voweling of the hamza-wāw interchange preserves meaning while reflecting distinct dialectal pronunciation traditions.
rows.anchor: Alternate voweling patterns for the hamza-waw interchange — canonical variants preserving meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sukūn on zāy lightens pronunciation while retaining explicit hamza and the same meaning.
rows.anchor: Sukun on za' — lightened pronunciation with explicit hamza; no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām-vowel variant contrasts mafʿal, which foregrounds the time of destruction, with mafʿil, which can foreground its manner or place.
rows.anchor: fatḥa on the lām instead of kasra (mahLAKihim vs mahLIKihim). mahLAK follows the mafʿal pattern

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The muhlak form shifts from intransitive perishing to passive or causative being destroyed, foregrounding external agency.
rows.anchor: Shifts the meaning from their perishing (intransitive, Form I mahlik) to their being-destroyed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza is pronounced in a simplified form, with no semantic change.
rows.anchor: Hamza variant — simplified hamza pronunciation, no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lengthened alif replaces hamza as a phonological variant with no semantic difference.
rows.anchor: Lengthened alif replaces hamza — phonological variant with no semantic difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Complete hamza elision streamlines pronunciation without changing the meaning.
rows.anchor: Complete hamza elision — streamlined pronunciation, same meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Canonical kasra and ḍamma readings of the final pronoun differ phonologically; kasra follows the preceding yāʾ while ḍamma preserves the independent pronoun form.
rows.anchor: Both are canonical readings. The kasra follows the yā' of -nī more naturally

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restoring the final yāʾ gives the full grammatical spelling rather than the Quranic pausal orthography, without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Restoring the final yā' — no semantic change but shifts from Quranic orthographic convention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sukūn-on-ghayn form with attached yāʾ is a variant pause form reflecting recitation differences between pausal and continuous reading.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on the ghayn with yā' attached in continuation — a variant pause form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source records no reading variant for this word in the verse.
rows.anchor: No recorded variants for this word in this ayah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Retaining the full yāʾ spells out the first-person object pronoun rather than eliding it; meaning is unchanged.
rows.anchor: Full yā' retained; no change in meaning, only orthographic/phonetic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant shows both pause and continuation forms, an orthographic distinction only.
rows.anchor: Variant with both forms showing the pause (waqf) and continuation (wasl) forms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rushd and rashad vowels distinguish inward maturity from the right course of outward action, though both are canonical.
rows.anchor: Lane's distinguishes rushd (right way/maturity of mind) from rashad (right course of action)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readers shorten the attached yāʾ in maʿī rather than reading maʿiya; the change affects prosody, not meaning.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with shortened yā (maʿī instead of maʿiya) — changes prosody but not meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source records no reading variant for this word.
rows.anchor: No recorded variants for this word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic nūn and gemination intensify the prohibition as “do not ever ask me.”
rows.anchor: Energetic nūn + gemination creates emphasis — ""do not ever ask me"" — intensifies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation of the final nūn adds phonetic emphasis while preserving the jussive.
rows.anchor: Variant with final nūn assimilated — produces phonetic emphasis while maintaining jussive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intransitive reading means the people drown, shifting agency away from al-Khiḍr and toward circumstance.
rows.anchor: Canonical Seven variant: intransitive ""so that [the people] drown"" rather than transitive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nominative ahluhā is subject of intransitive yaghraqa; accusative ahlahā is object of transitive tughriqa.
rows.anchor: nominative ahluhā as subject of intransitive yaghraqa -- ""so its people drown"" vs accusative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shortened yāʾ in maʿī is a canonical phonological variant without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: shortened yāʾ (maʿī instead of maʿiya) -- phonological difference only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant replaces hamza with wāw in tuʾākhidhnī, simplifying pronunciation without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Hamza replacement: tuʾākhidhnī → tuwākhidhnī; hamza replaced by wāw

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding ḍamma on sīn produces fuʿulun rather than fuʿlun; both forms mean hardship, while ʿusuran may be more intensive.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: ʿusran → ʿusuran; additional ḍamma on sīn creates fuʿulun pattern

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zākiya as an active participle suggests ongoing purification, while zakiyya presents an established state of full purity.
rows.anchor: Active participle (fāʿila) vs standard intensive (faʿīla): zākiya = actively purifying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fuller nukuran pronunciation changes phonetic weight, not meaning, and matches the gravity of the charge.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: nukran (sukūn on kāf) → nukuran (ḍamma on kāf) — does not change meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical shortened-yāʾ variant concerns the adjacent word maʿiya; the source refers to word 8.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant affecting the adjacent word maʿiya — vowel shortening on the yā' of maʿī (see word 8)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shortening the final vowel yields maʿī instead of maʿiya; the meaning remains identical.
rows.anchor: Canonical reading shortening the final vowel — maʿī instead of maʿiya. The semantic meaning is identical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The single-nūn form without tashdīd is a lighter grammatical form meaning “from my presence.”
rows.anchor: Single nūn (without tashdīd); lighter grammatical form, same meaning - from my presence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A short ḍamma on dāl changes pronunciation but not meaning.
rows.anchor: With short ḍamma on dāl; phonological variant affecting pronunciation but not meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on dāl compresses the word to two syllables.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on dāl; reduces the word to two syllables; more compressed form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form I takhidha instead of Form VIII ittakhadha means simply “you took,” without the reflexive self-benefiting nuance.
rows.anchor: Form I takhidha instead of Form VIII ittakhadha — simpler ""you took"" without the reflexive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form II baddala rather than Form IV intensifies the replacement, suggesting a repeated or thorough exchange.
rows.anchor: Form II (baddala) instead of Form IV (abdala) — intensifies the act of replacing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruḥuman versus ruḥman differs in vowel pattern; fuʿul can suggest greater intensity or fullness without a major semantic shift.
rows.anchor: Vowel change on the second radical — ruḥuman vs ruḥman; may suggest a slightly different morphological form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form VIII stresses Dhū al-Qarnayn's personal choice and adherence, while Form IV stresses deliberate active pursuit; both are canonical.
rows.anchor: Form VIII ittabaʿa (reflexive-intensive) vs standard Form IV atbaʿa (causative). VIII emphasizes personal choice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active participle from ḥ-m-y describes a hot or heated spring instead of a dark muddy one.
rows.anchor: active participle from ḥ-m-y ""to be hot, to protect"" — shifts description from dark-muddy to hot/heated spring

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fuller nukuran and shorter nukran are semantically equivalent canonical readings, though nukuran carries greater phonetic weight.
rows.anchor: Vowel change: ḍamma on kāf (nukuran) vs. sukūn (nukran). The fuller vowel form nukuran may be

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nominative iḍāfa makes jazāʾ the subject and al-ḥusnā its genitive complement, forming “the recompense of the best.”
rows.anchor: Nominative iḍāfa: ""the recompense OF the best"" — jazāʾ becomes mubtadaʾ (subject)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full ḍamma on sīn is a phonological or dialectal variant of yusran with the same root and meaning.
rows.anchor: Vocalization variant: full ḍamma on sīn (yusuran) instead of sukūn (yusran); same root

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form VIII emphasizes deliberate personal following, whereas Form IV stresses causation and active pursuit; both are canonical.
rows.anchor: Form VIII (iftaʿala) instead of Form IV (afʿala) — shifts from causative ""he caused to follow / he pursued""

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Form VIII reading presents Dhū al-Qarnayn as choosing to follow personally, rather than causing another to follow; several of the Seven read it.
rows.anchor: Form VIII (iftaʿala) reading — reflexive-intensive: he deliberately followed, chose to follow

rows.speaker: al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿAmr
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿAmr read al-suddayni with ḍamma, which the source interprets as divinely placed barriers, unlike the fatḥa reading's human-made structures.
rows.anchor: classical grammarians (al-Kisāʾī, Abū ʿAmr) read with ḍamma, implying divinely-placed barriers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Form IV reading yufqihūna means they can scarcely make others understand speech, shifting from inability to understand to inability to convey.
rows.anchor: Form IV causative: yufqihūna = ""they can scarcely make [others] understand speech"" — shifts from receptive incomprehension

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dropping the hamza in Yājūj smooths pronunciation and, if hamza reflects the root ʾ-j-j, obscures the derivation associated with blazing.
rows.anchor: Hamza dropped: yaʾjūj → yājūj — removes the glottal stop, yielding smoother pronunciation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A paired variant drops hamza in both names, maintaining phonological symmetry between Yājūj and Mājūj.
rows.anchor: Paired variant: both names lose hamza simultaneously — maʾjūj → mājūj; the pair maintains phonological symmetry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lengthened kharāj means a systematic tax or tribute, while kharj suggests a one-time expenditure, changing the offer's fiscal character.
rows.anchor: Variant with alif-lengthening: kharāj = systematic tax/tribute vs. kharj = one-time expenditure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The classical distinction assigns ḍamma sudd to natural or divine barriers and fatḥa sadd to human-built barriers.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: sudd (ḍamma) vs. sadd (fatḥa) — classical distinction assigns sudd to natural/divine barriers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Preserving the full nūn in makkananī rather than assimilating it increases phonetic clarity without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Full nun preserved without assimilation — makkana + nī becomes makkananī instead of makkannī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A boundary variant attaches “bring me” to 18:95 rather than 18:96, changing whether the iron request belongs to this verse and the scope of Dhū al-Qarnayn's promise.
rows.anchor: Variant affects the boundary between 18:95 and 18:96: some readings attach ātūnī (bring me) to this ayah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form I iʾtūnī means come to me carrying iron, emphasizing workers' physical participation; Form IV ātūnī means bring it, emphasizing delivery.
rows.anchor: Variant reads Form I imperative iʾtūnī ""come to me [with]"" instead of Form IV ātūnī ""bring me.""

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on dāl gives ṣudf rather than ṣadaf; both denote a cliff face or shell, with a different dialectal vowel pattern.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on dāl: ṣudf instead of ṣadaf. Same meaning (cliff-face/shell), different dialectal voweling

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The double-ḍamma ṣuduf form still denotes cliff faces but may reflect a different or intensive morphological pattern.
rows.anchor: Double ḍamma: ṣuduf. This pattern (fuʿul) may indicate a different plural base or intensive form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the qāla boundary, loss of the final vowel produces Form I iʾtūnī, “come to me,” instead of Form IV “bring me.”
rows.anchor: Variant affects boundary between qāla and ātūnī: in one reading qāla loses final vowel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As above, Form I means come to me with material, while Form IV means bring it; ātūnī may also imply bringing molten copper or coming so Dhū al-Qarnayn can pour.
rows.anchor: Same variant as word 1: Form I ""come to me [with]"" vs Form IV ""bring me."" Here the second

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full assimilation of tāʾ into ṭāʾ produces a heavier articulation that emphasizes effort.
rows.anchor: Full assimilation of tāʾ into ṭāʾ — iṭṭāʿa pattern, heavier articulation emphasizing the effort

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without hamza the word is an indefinite verbal noun, emphasizing the act of leveling rather than the resulting flat state described by dakkāʾ.
rows.anchor: Without hamza, indeterminate/indefinite noun — shifts from dakkāʾ (adjective: ""level/flat"") to dakkan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatḥa on the final yāʾ in dūniya is a pause or continuation phonetic variant without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Variant adds fatḥa on final yāʾ (dūniya vs dūnī) — phonetic variant in pause/continuation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading preserves hamza explicitly rather than softening it to wāw; both are canonical and semantically alike.
rows.anchor: Hamza preserved explicitly rather than softened to wāw — هُزُءًا vs هُزُوًا; both canonical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several canonical vocalizations vary in sukūn and hamza/wāw treatment but are purely phonetic variants.
rows.anchor: Multiple variant vocalizations of the same root — sukūn on zāy with different hamza/wāw treatments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ten-reader variant combines sukūn on zāy with explicit hamza for a lighter pronunciation.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on zāy with explicit hamza — 10-reader variant combining lighter pronunciation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine yanfada agrees with treating kalimāt as a broken plural, which can take masculine agreement.
rows.anchor: Masculine form yanfada instead of feminine tanfada — treating kalimāt as a broken plural

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical bare form recites the opening letter names continuously without pause marks.
rows.anchor: Canonical bare form — letter-names recited as continuous unit without pause marks

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A canonical extended form has dhikru follow the disjoint letters.
rows.anchor: Canonical extended form — dhikru follows the letter-string; seven-reading canonical variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imāla variant tilts the hāʾ and yāʾ vowels toward /e/.
rows.anchor: Imāla variant — hāʾ and yāʾ vowels tilted toward /e/; canonical seven-reading variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A vowel variant pronounces yāʾ with kasra as ye.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant — yāʾ pronounced with kasra (ye); canonical seven-reading variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assimilation variant assimilates final ṣād to the dhāl of dhikru.
rows.anchor: Assimilation variant — ṣād's final consonant assimilates to the dh of dhikru

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A vowel variant pronounces hāʾ with kasra as he.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant — hāʾ pronounced with kasra (he); canonical seven-reading variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imāla variant gives both hāʾ and yāʾ kasra vowels.
rows.anchor: Imāla variant — both hāʾ and yāʾ with kasra vowels; canonical seven-reading variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ten-reader waqf variant marks each letter with an explicit pause, reciting them as separate units.
rows.anchor: Ten-reading waqf variant — each letter marked with explicit pause; letters individuated as separate recitation units

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation of final ṣād to the following dhāl is phonological only and leaves meaning unchanged.
rows.anchor: Phonological assimilation of ṣād (end of kāf-hā-yā-ʿayn-ṣād) to following dhāl — no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name Zakariyyāʾ is read with terminal hamza, treating the final alif as hamza-bearing and matching the Hebrew -yāh ending; both forms are canonical.
rows.anchor: Adds a terminal hamza to the name — treats final alif as hamza-bearing; consistent with Hebrew transliteration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard reading has long ā and hamza followed by the possessive yāʾ.
rows.anchor: Standard canonical reading with long ā and hamza; final yāʾ is possessive suffix

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical variant opens the final syllable as -ya; both readings belong to the seven canonical readings.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with final -ya (open syllable); both are within 7 canonical readings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jussive forms of both inheritance verbs frame the request as a petition or condition rather than a confident assertion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second inheritance verb is likewise jussive, reinforcing the petitionary mood of both verbs.
rows.anchor: Apocoped jussive: paired with يَرِثْنِي — both verbs in jussive, reinforcing petitionary mood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding hamza to Zakariyyā supplies nominative case inflection and links the name continuously to innā.
rows.anchor: Hamza added at end of Zakariyyā (Zakariyyāʾu), giving it case inflection (nominative)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same hamza addition is paired with a marked pause or phonological break before innā.
rows.anchor: Same hamza addition; •اِنَّا shows a deliberate pause or phonological break before innā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form I nabshuru replaces Form II nubashshiru, reducing the verb to a simpler form rather than an intensive heralding.
rows.anchor: Form I (nabshuru) instead of Form II (nubashshiru): verb form reduced — simpler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Changing the first-syllable vowel from ī to ū preserves the meaning of extreme age but gives it heavier phonetic weight.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift ī → ū on first syllable; same root ʿ-t-w, same meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural “We created you” replaces singular “I created you,” changing the pronoun from personal intimacy to majestic plural while preserving the action.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant (7-reading tradition): first-person plural ""We created you"" vs. singular

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An open yāʾ rather than lī is a canonical phonological variant without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Variant with open yāʾ (liya vs lī); both canonical 7-reader tradition

rows.speaker: author

rows.anchor: Standard form with final long ī; pausal form of inna + pronoun suffix

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final -a on yāʾ preserves the full vowel sequence in non-pausal recitation without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Short vowel -a on final yāʾ; non-pausal pronunciation preserving full vowel chain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yahaba instead of ahaba makes God, rather than the angel, the grammatical subject of granting.
rows.anchor: Variant replaces 1S ahaba with 3MS yahaba: God (not the angel) is the grammatical subject

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍamma on mīm is a canonical dialectal variant of the first-person perfect of m-w-t with the same meaning.
rows.anchor: Ḍamma on mīm — dialectal variant of 1s perfect of m-w-t; same meaning

rows.speaker: author

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading man as a relative pronoun instead of min as a preposition makes the one beneath Mary the caller, identifying the infant as subject.
rows.anchor: مَنْ (relative pronoun ""who/the one"") replaces مِنْ (preposition ""from""); تَحْتَهَا shifts to accusative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form VI jussive second-person feminine makes Mary the agent who shakes the palm and causes fruit to cascade down.
rows.anchor: Form VI impf jussive 2fs — Mary is agent; she shakes and causes cascading drop

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form V with initial tāʾ assimilated makes the palm the agent, so fruit drops of itself rather than by Mary's active causation.
rows.anchor: Form V with initial ta-assimilation to sā; palm is agent — fruit drops of itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form VI third-person feminine makes the palm the agent in progressive or successive dropping.
rows.anchor: Form VI 3fs (short vowel on ta-); palm (fem) is agent; progressive or successive dropping

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A masculine-subject Form V or VI reading has an unnamed masculine agent causing or experiencing cascading, possibly God.
rows.anchor: Form V/VI with masculine subject (3ms): unnamed masculine agent causes or experiences cascading

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard open yāʾ in ātāniya is shortened or elided at pause in ātānī; this is phonological only.
rows.anchor: Standard form ātāniya has final open yāʾ (yāʾ mutaḥarrika); variant ātānī drops the final vowel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard accusative qawla is a cognate object, functioning as mafʿūl muṭlaq for an implied qāla.
rows.anchor: Standard form: accusative gerund; qawla = mafʿūl muṭlaq of implied qāla

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative qawlu becomes a second predicate of dhālika, yielding “that is ʿĪsā ... and the word of truth.”
rows.anchor: Canonical variant (also 7-reader): nominative; qawlu l-ḥaqqi becomes second predicate of dhālika

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Indicative yakūnu asserts that the thing comes into existence as an immediate ontological fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subjunctive yakūna reads the command “Be!” purposively, marking coming into being as its goal rather than immediate factual outcome.
rows.anchor: Variant reading: yakūna in nasb (subjunctive) — purposive reading: God says ""Be!"" so that it may come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard inna is asseverative, with its noun in the accusative.
rows.anchor: Standard canonical: inna (asseverative), noun in accusative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anna as complementizer embeds the clause as the object of an implied verb: it was declared that God is my Lord.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: anna (complementizer), embeds clause as object of implied verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard ṣād is emphatic and heavy, giving the word a solemn sound.
rows.anchor: Standard: ṣād — emphatic sibilant, heavy and solemn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical sīn variant is a lighter sibilant with the same root, shifting phonetic register.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with sīn — lighter sibilant; same root, phonetic register shifts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalaf from Ḥamza reads ṣād tilted toward zāy, an intermediate articulation.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with ṣād tilted toward zāy — intermediate sound between ṣ and z

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard passive plural means “they are returned,” suppressing but implying divine agency.
rows.anchor: Standard 7-canonical passive 3rd pl: ""they are returned"" — divine agent suppressed but implied

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active third-person plural means “they return,” making the returnees self-directed agents rather than passive objects.
rows.anchor: 7-canonical ACTIVE 3rd pl: ""they return"" — removes the passive; returnees are self-directed agents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The long ā variant in Ibrāhīm is a Hijazi form closer to the Semitic original Avraham.
rows.anchor: Long vowel shift ī→ā in second syllable; Hijazi form closer to Semitic original Avraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard kasra on tāʾ is treated as a stabilized vocative ending.
rows.anchor: Kasra on tāʾ: standard reading (canonical); tāʾ with kasra as stabilized vocative ending

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternate canonical fatḥa may reflect an accusative-like ending or another vocalization tradition for the vocative tāʾ.
rows.anchor: Fatḥa on tāʾ: alternate canonical reading; fatḥa may reflect an accusative-like case ending

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatḥa instead of kasra changes the vocative ending from an imāla-prone form to one reflecting a different regional prosodic tradition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sīn replaces ṣād through phonetic interchange; the source links it to s-r-ṭ, “to swallow,” evoking a path that swallows the traveler.
rows.anchor: sīn replaces ṣād; phonetic interchange s/ṣ; links to root s-r-ṭ ""to swallow"" — the path that swallows

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣād with a zayn marker represents an intermediate articulation between ṣād and zāy.
rows.anchor: ṣād with zayn-diacritical marker (ṣ → ṣᶻ); intermediate articulation between ṣ and z

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatḥa on tāʾ rather than the more common kasra is also canonical in the seven readings.
rows.anchor: Fatḥa on tāʾ instead of kasra; both canonical (seven readings); the kasra (abati) is more common

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both kasra abati and fatḥa abata are canonical; the tāʾ in the fixed vocative “yā abati” is tāʾ al-taʾnīth.
rows.anchor: Standard reading: kasra on tāʾ (abati); variant: fatḥa on tāʾ (abata) — both canonical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The open final yāʾ in inniya and shortened innī are both canonical prosodic variants, with no semantic difference.
rows.anchor: Standard: innī (yāʾ with sukūn/shortened); variant: inniya (yāʾ with fatḥa, open vowel)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority's standard form Ibrāhīmu has long ī in the third syllable.
rows.anchor: Standard form: long ī in third syllable (Ibrā-hī-mu); canonical reading of the majority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical variant lengthens the third-syllable vowel to ā rather than ī, reflecting variation in transmission of the name.
rows.anchor: Variant: long ā in third syllable (Ibrā-hā-mu) instead of ī; both canonical (7-readings)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full voweling of the final yāʾ is a canonical phonological variant with the same meaning.
rows.anchor: Full voweling of the final yāʾ — same semantic content, differs only in phonological realization

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard Form IV passive participle presents God as having chosen or purified Moses.
rows.anchor: Standard: Form IV passive participle — God chose/purified Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active Form IV participle presents Moses as devoting or purifying himself.
rows.anchor: Variant: Form IV active participle — Moses devotes/purifies himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ten-reader tradition marks hamza differently in Isrāʾīl without semantic change.
rows.anchor: The 10-reader tradition marks the hamza position differently; type hmz (hamza treatment). No semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard canonical reading has ḍamma on bāʾ in bukiyyan.
rows.anchor: Standard canonical reading: wa-bukiyyan with ḍamma on bāʾ — attested as canonical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra on bāʾ gives bikiyyan; both kasra and ḍamma readings are canonical and have no semantic distinction.
rows.anchor: Alternate vowel: kasra on bāʾ (bikiyyan instead of bukiyyan) — also canonical in 7-reader tradition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active imperfect depicts them entering by their own agency.
rows.anchor: Active imperfect (3pl): they enter by their own agency — entry as self-performed act

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive imperfect depicts them being brought in, shifting agency to God and making entry divinely conferred.
rows.anchor: Passive imperfect (3pl): they are brought in — agency shifts to God; entry is divinely conferred

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Standard Form IV nūrithu means “we cause to inherit”; the object, al-jannata, is elided and co-referential with the nominal sentence's subject.
rows.anchor: Standard Form IV awratha imperfect 1pl: we cause to inherit; object (al-jannata) elided

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form II nuwarrithu means “we bequeath” and foregrounds God's deliberate assignment rather than the recipient's status as heir.
rows.anchor: Canonical Form II warrattha imperfect 1pl: we bequeath/assign as inheritance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dialectal ḍamma on mīm instead of kasra permits muttu alongside mittu without semantic difference.
rows.anchor: ḍamma on mīm instead of kasra: dialectal hollow-verb PV 1cs vowel alternation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form V with tāʾ assimilated into dhāl presents remembering as deliberate self-reflection; its heavier sound mirrors the effort the audience fails to make.
rows.anchor: Form V with assimilation of tā into dhāl (yatadhakkaru → yadhdhakkaru); shifts reproach from basic recall

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jīm vowel alternates between ḍamma and standard kasra in canonical readings, possibly reflecting a distinct broken-plural pattern without semantic difference.
rows.anchor: ḍamma on jīm (juthiyyan) vs standard kasra (jithiyyan); both canonical 7-reader chains

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both canonical ʿutiyyan and ʿitiyyan derive from ʿ-t-w and mean extreme rebellion; the vowel shift may reflect dialectal phonology.
rows.anchor: both are canonical 7-reading chains; the Hafs reading is ʿitiyyan (kasra); the ḍamma variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spatial thamma (“there”) replaces temporal “then,” portraying rescue from within Hell's space rather than in a later phase and dramatizing the proximity of rescue and damnation.
rows.anchor: Spatial adverb ""there"" replaces temporal conjunction ""then"" — God rescues from within Hell's space

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard reading retains hamza in riʾyan, forming a glottal break in the noun for outward appearance.
rows.anchor: Standard canonical reading; hamza retained creating glottal break; root r-ʾ-y; noun riʾy = outward appearance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second canonical reading drops hamza and doubles yāʾ by assimilation, with the same root and meaning but smoother phonology.
rows.anchor: Hamza dropped, yāʾ doubled by assimilation; same root and meaning; second 7-canonical reading

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Facilitating hamza drops it from raʾā for lighter pronunciation while retaining the same grammatical meaning.
rows.anchor: Hamza facilitation — hamza of raʾā dropped entirely; phonologically lighter; grammatically identical meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The marked transitional hamza represents an intermediate sound between full realization and full elision, reflecting early dialectal variation.
rows.anchor: Hamza rest/transitional — hamza marked as a middle phonological state between full realization and full drop

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prolonging hamza to a long ā creates an emphatic pause before the relative clause and stretches the interrogative moment.
rows.anchor: Hamza prolonged into long ā vowel; creates emphatic pause before the relative clause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The split pause-and-continuation double reading presents hamza as a live phonological question in early transmission.
rows.anchor: Split waqf/waṣl double-reading variant; unusual form suggesting hamza was a live phonological question

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wuld is a collective offspring noun, intensifying the boast from one heir to a dynasty rather than one child.
rows.anchor: Vowel change: wuld (collective plural) — offspring as a group/mass noun; intensifies the boast

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wuldan is collective progeny rather than singular waladan, shifting from an individual child to descendants as a group without changing the root.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: waladan (a-a-an, singular concrete noun) → wuldan (u-∅-an, collective/plural form)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Masculine yakādu replaces feminine takādu, treating al-samāwāt as masculine or restructuring the clause impersonally.
rows.anchor: Masculine form (yakādu) instead of feminine takādu — subject al-samāwāt treated as masculine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form VII yanfaṭirna favors a single completed split over the progressive or iterative rupture of Form V yatafaṭṭarna; compare 82:1.
rows.anchor: Form VII instead of Form V — yanfaṭirna (infaṭara) vs. yatafaṭṭarna (tafaṭṭara)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural wuldan amplifies the transgression from a claim about one child to offspring in general.
rows.anchor: Plural form ""offspring/children"" vs. singular ""a child"" — amplifies the transgression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Collective wuldan shifts the claim from one specific child to offspring as a category; it is a canonical variant.
rows.anchor: wuldan (collective plural ""progeny/offspring collectively"") vs. standard waladan (singular ""a child"")

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form I tabshura removes doubled shin from Form II tubashshira, shifting from solemn heralding to plain informing.
rows.anchor: Form I (tabshura) vs. Form II (tubashshira) — removes doubled shin; simpler announcement
